CEO, Banco Santander
Okay. Spanish banking tax. Unfortunately, I have no idea, yeah, at this moment at this point of time. I was told that the rumor in the media is that this morning, the same morning, we're gonna have a kind of presentation because this is a presentation in the parliament for the parties, for coming from the parties. This is the way they manage this, and we're gonna know this the same morning. If this affect Spanish operations or global operations, I have no idea. I do expect that this affect Spanish operations, but we'll see what happens when this is presented to the parliament today. ALCO in Spain, we don't have ALCO in Spain, zero. We don't have bonds.
You are asking me for the level of potential ALCO portfolio. Well, if I look at, we have a negative duration of five years in the balance sheet in Spain. If you were to offset all of this, the portfolio will be very, very large, yeah? So you can do the math on your own, but it will be very large. But what seems to me is a reasonable ALCO portfolio for Spain is to put the duration of the balance sheet between the minus two and plus two years, yeah? That is normally where we imagine the portfolio, except in extraordinary times when the rates went into negative territory.
We're gonna reconstruct this portfolio little by little, depending on our view on the market and trying to put the balance sheet with a less negative duration. We haven't started, but we will for sure start at some point when we think is the appropriate time. Banamex, well, as you know, we've been very transparent on this. We're interested in the asset. We put the conditions. One of the conditions was at the price, naturally, at the price. The return on investment was in conditions not to issue shares. We told you openly, we submit a non-binding offer and, well, we were told that we are not going to continue in the process. That's it. There is no more to add, yeah?
Well, as I said before to your colleague, we think that we put a price asking for a return on investment attractive for our shareholders, knowing that we have a good chance of gaining market share in the new situation and growing organically and adding several percentage points of market share in Mexico with our existing franchise.
Sofie Peterzens
Executive Director, JPMorgan
Thank you.
Begoña Morenes
Global Head of Investor Relations, Banco Santander
Thank you, Sofie. Can we have the next question, please?
Operator
The next question is coming from Benjie Creelan-Sandford from Jefferies. Please go ahead.
Benjie Creelan-Sandford
Banks Analyst, Jefferies
Yes. Good morning, everyone. Thanks for taking the questions. I had two questions on the revenue outlook, please. First of all, just on the Digital Consumer Bank, you know, I guess looking in the quarter, volumes are going up, but margins are going down. So just wondering if you could discuss a little bit about what you're seeing in terms of consumer loan demand, across the European business. You know, how are clients reacting to cost of living pressures versus, you know, what are still very good employment trends. In terms of margins in the consumer business, you know, is there a lag effect in terms of asset repricing that is weighing on margins, or are you seeing increasing pricing competition in that segment?
The second question was just a clarification on Brazil and the NII outlook in H2. So I understood that you expect the, sort of the repricing, the rate repricing to sort of level out in Q4. Should we assume that NII will be down sequentially in Q3 again? Perhaps if you could just be a bit more precise, or offer any more guidance around kind of the rebound, as the lag effect in the rate repricing runs off into 2023. I know you gave guidance on the rate sensitivity on a year one basis. Can you give any indication of what that rate sensitivity looks like on a year two basis in Brazil? Thank you.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Okay. The first question, let me to elaborate on Digital Consumer Bank, consumer loan demand in Europe. The consumer loan demand is not bad, I should say. It's good. Yeah. The problem with it, our portfolio here is basically EUR 120 million, of which EUR 85 billion.
EUR 120 billion, of which EUR 85 billion or north of EUR 85 billion is related with auto and the remaining is basically direct lending and point of sales. We are seeing good trends in both business, but lead times in the auto industry are getting very, very long. To give you a proxy of this, normally we have a stock financing that funds the inventory of the car dealers, normally in the region of EUR 13 to 15 billion. Now this is running at half of this. It's EUR 6 to 7 billion. This tells you an indication where the industry is in the capacity to deliver the demand they have. On the other side, I mentioned for the US, but the same happens in Europe, the activity in used car markets and the price in used car markets is strong.
Our origination this year, we're going to go to the EUR 50 billion mark. This is where our originations are growing 10%, but this is because we are gaining share, okay? It's not. The market is not there. Car sales are falling significantly. What happens is we are gaining share all across, and for that reason, we are growing 10% originations. The second question, this is the situation of the market. The second question was margin and pricing. This business, let me start with the balance sheet of this business. This business is, as I said, close to a EUR 120 billion loan book. The majority of this is fixed rate, normally with a duration of around two years.
Funded with a combination of deposits in the region of EUR 40 billion, and the rest is wholesale funding, normally, insurance and securitizations and other things, while we tend to have relatively very low interest rate risk in this business. What is happening with the margins? Yields are going up, not at the speed of the what is happening in the swap yield curve, but this is the usual pattern that this business follow. Normally, it started to go up a couple of months ago, more so in countries in which the rates went up faster, before, like UK and the other markets are following. I don't see a pattern now differently than the one I was expecting.
Normally, this business suffer a little bit, not that much, because the combination of 40% deposits and 60% wholesale funding, the majority of this with around two years duration. We can accommodate the majority of this and not to suffer that much on the margin side. The fee income is doing well on the other side, on the back of the activity. If the activity recovers, I do not expect a significant margin compression there. Although this, we cannot pass 100% the very first day. We pass over a period of three to four months the new prices to the new origination. In Brazil, you mentioned NII outlook, the Q4 and rebound in Brazil, when rebound is gonna happen. José gave you some indications of this.
Basically, what happens in Brazil, as long as rates go up. Let me explain the NII in Brazil. NII in Brazil, in the loan book is going up. It went up, has been going up. In the market-related activities collapsed and went into negative territory. The rates went from 2% to 12%. When this is gonna turn around? Normally, when you finish the tightening cycle, it takes around two quarters to go up. We think that we are close to the peak, but we will see. We think that is a couple of basis points still to come from the Central Bank of Brazil, probably 75, probably 100, I don't know, in this region. Two quarters afterwards, we gonna show up this in NII.
José mentioned 2023 for the rebound, expecting that with the central bank rates, the official rate in Brazil peaks.
José García Cantera
CFO and Senior EVP, Banco Santander
In August.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Peaks August, September this year. Okay? This is our outlook for Brazil. Having said that, the customer business, so the loan book, the spread of the loan book is going up. The financial activities went from positive territory to negative territory this year and is the main swing we have there. This is gonna fade away as long as the portfolio mature and renew all these things. Yeah. Those are the dynamics in Brazil.
Begoña Morenes
Global Head of Investor Relations, Banco Santander
Thank you, José Antonio. Thank you, Benjie, for your question. Can we have the next one, please?
Operator
The next question is coming from Ignacio Cerezo from UBS. Please go ahead.
Ignacio Cerezo
Equity Research Analyst, UBS
Yeah. Hi, good morning. Thank you for the presentation. I have two questions on the US, both around asset quality. So if you can kind of let us know your view about what we need to monitor to gauge when and how quickly asset quality can start deteriorating, if it's unemployment, like you were mentioning, the European consumer finance operation, or you're also concerned around collateral prices going down and reversing the pickup we have seen in the last couple of years. The second question around this is, I mean, obviously the units, well, it has been blended into one. I mean, we don't have the disclosure between SCUSA and the rest of the bank any longer, and there has been significant changes on the mix of SCUSA in recent years as well.
It's difficult for us actually to have a kind of a realistic view of the through-the-cycle cost of risk for the unit. If you can share with us your view, basically, on where the cost of risk in the US can actually land in a normal environment. Thank you.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Okay. The first question about asset quality, what we are looking when this start deteriorating, natural unemployment rate is one of the key drivers also in the US. You mentioned us, what is going on. Let me guide you a little bit what's going on in SCUSA in terms of the dynamics of the business now. We are seeing a significant. We are generating in the loan book with a FICO that is 35 points above what we were generating one year ago. So this is, we're generating this. The pricing model is quite sophisticated and goes along with the FICOs we are generating. So this explain a little bit the trends in yields there.
Second, leasing business now, the dynamics are different from any time we've ever seen before. Normally, leasing businesses work in a way that the customers take the car and three years later or four years later, they give us back the car and we dispose the car in an auction to the market. This process in normal times is a process that produces very little profits, very little losses. What has happened along this period is in 2021, this was a very profitable business in 2020 on the back of very high second-hand used car market price. But in 2022, what we're seeing is the customers are not returning back the cars to us. They prefer to selling their own, given the high prices prevailing in the used car markets. This changed the dynamics in the P&L.
Is that the reason that you see that the I think it's in the other income, you see a significant decrease in the other income due to this phenomena. Last year, we made out of this EUR 200 million, this year we are making very little out of this process. Asset quality, we expect, we traditionally were around 4% or 4-something percent in SCUSA. In the cost of risk, less than 5%. Now the cost of risk in US, the whole US, is 1.5%. What the bank is, you split between the bank. The bank is very low cost of risk. It's meaningless.
All the cost of risk you are seeing now, the 1.5% comes from SCUSA, okay? This normalization will happen over time, and it depends not necessarily on the past. As we are generating higher FICO scores, we also expect lower cost of risk when the unemployment deteriorate. I think unemployment continues to be the main driver, not as much as interest rates. Remember that we here are lending a very high yield, and the impact of additional 100 basis points or 50 or 200 basis points in the yield is not meaningful when you are lending at 20% or something like that. Auto to 21 is not as important as it is in the prime space, where the changes in the rates can produce more significant changes in the monthly installments. I think I answer your questions, yeah.
Begoña Morenes
Global Head of Investor Relations, Banco Santander
Thank you, José Antonio, and thank you, Ignacio, for your questions. Can we have the next question, please?
Operator
The next question is coming from Carlos Peixoto from CaixaBank. Please go ahead.
Carlos Peixoto
Senior Director of Equity Research, CaixaBank
Yes. Hi, hi, good morning. A couple of questions from my side as well. I was just wondering, and well, the first one is really just a follow-up, but because I believe I missed exactly the guidance that you had given for NII in Brazil for the full year. On the second question, I was wondering on the outlook for cost of risk in Spain. I believe that in the past you had mentioned something in the areas of 50 basis points. Right now, cost of risk is still trending a bit above those levels. I was wondering how you see it for the second half of the year and possibly to 2023. Thank you.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
NII in Brazil in H2 of the year. A mid-single digit growth in Brazil is what you should expect for NII in Brazil for the whole year. While the cost of risk in Spain hasn't changed our expectations we set 50 to 60 basis points for the whole year. Probably this is what you should expect for Spain this year. While naturally this means, as you know, the cost of risk now largely depends on the macro scenarios? Well, I told you that EUR 600 million in H1 came from the macro. Well, the H2, the macro is so uncertain in these days that well, we will see what kind of macro we introduce at the end of the year.
If the macro remains as it is today, let's take IMF expectations that they published yesterday, day before yesterday, should stay in these levels, yeah. As I said to you before, we do not expect a big deal this year on the ground coming from the cost of risk, yeah.
Begoña Morenes
Global Head of Investor Relations, Banco Santander
Thank you, José Antonio. Thank you, Carlos, for your questions. Can we have the next one, please?
Operator
The next question is coming from Andrea Filtri from Mediobanca. Please go ahead.
Andrea Filtri
Co-Head of Research, Mediobanca
Thank you. Two questions. One on rate sensitivity. This is the flavor of the moment, but the visibility you're giving is still quite low compared to other names. Can you please give us for each main area your 12-month rate sensitivity, assuming zero deposit beta, if you plugged in the forward curve that we can all see, just to add some transparency on that front? I didn't understand quite well before, José Antonio, your elaboration around the reason not to have any Spanish bonds, ALCO portfolio in Spain and how big the ALCO should be in a normalized scenario. The second question is on Brazil, again, on the rate sensitivity.
You elaborated quite a lot around this, but I wanted to understand in Brazilian reais term what you would expect then to be the tailwind on a full phasing when the liability repricing stops and asset repricing at the current rates level is completed to understand the- Does the pendulum swing from the negative headwind to the positive tailwind, and hence, how much can this play in terms of cost of risk? Thank you.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Okay. Let me elaborate. José will guide you through the specific details on numbers you see. Rates, sensitivity to rates. Yeah, so we're gonna give you an easy representation, the parallel shift on the yield curve, but you ask for areas. High level, I should say that with the forward, normally what happens is this is a process that is accelerating. So if I take the whole 2023 with the forward rates, probably in Europe, we think we should think in all our business in Europe, EUR 2 billion, north of EUR 2 billion, probably. This is a figure that, well, you know, there is plenty of numbers there, but this is a figure that sounds reasonable to me.
You asked for the Spanish ALCO, well, I may in terms of duration, but having an ALCO between EUR 20 and 40 billion is something that sounds to me reasonable to. ALCO does not necessarily mean one single sovereign. Means a portfolio of fixed rate assets that we do not generate in commercial terms. In commercial terms, as you know, the majority of our 80% of the mortgage book, the majority of the lending to SMEs and corporates, and 100% of the lending to CIB or almost 100% of the lending to CIB is floating rate.
On the other way around is a limited asset that we generate a fixed rate, and for that reason, the need of having a significant ALCO portfolio in Spain, and we don't have because our view of our interest rates was that they should go up, and that's the reason why we don't have this portfolio. José, you want to-
José García Cantera
CFO and Senior EVP, Banco Santander
Yeah.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Clarify the specific data?
José García Cantera
CFO and Senior EVP, Banco Santander
Yeah. The reason we give a parallel shift. Well, parallel shift really is from one day to 12 months. The sensitivity we have doesn't go beyond 12 months, obviously. When we talk about a parallel shift, we are talking about a movement between overnight and 12 months. The reason we give a parallel shift is because today, for instance, the market is expecting rates in Europe to stay at 1%, while just a month ago, it was much higher than that. It's much better to look at sensitivity and then for a parallel shift, which is again a movement between a day and 12 months, and then you put your own, you know, outlook of rates.
For a parallel shift of 100 basis points and a 25% beta, the sensitivity in Spain is EUR 750 million, in the UK is EUR 300 million, most of which we have already seen, by the way. In the UK, we would expect further sensitivity in the H2 of this year, and then probably some stabilization in 2023, EUR 140 million in the US. For the second year, this is relevant for Brazil. In Brazil, in the second year, we would expect a positive sensitivity of around EUR 150 million.
If we are right, and then the last interest rate hike takes place in August, September, and then we start seeing the positive sensitivity flowing through the P&L in Brazil towards the end of this year, beginning of next year, then we should see the sensitivity in the P&L in Brazil, which is around EUR 140 to 150 million. This sensitivity to a parallel shift is in the presentation.
Begoña Morenes
Global Head of Investor Relations, Banco Santander
Thank you, José and José Antonio. Thank you, Andrea, for your question. Can we have the next one, please?
Operator
Just a quick reminder, to ask a question, press star one. The next question is coming from Carlos Cobo Catena from Societe Generale. Please go ahead.
Carlos Cobo Catena
Director of Equity Research, Societe Generale
Hi. Thank you very much for taking my questions. A couple of questions from me. One is on M&A appetite now that you've ruled out Mexico. There's been some reports in the media about you exploring some agreements or expanding the agreements with car makers in Europe. You've always been very interested in your consumer finance business. Could that be an area where you could do some bolt-on deals? How material, if you could quantify that, they might be in terms of capital consumption, if it's possible to give some view. I understand there's been some pop-ups in the macro provisions overlay. Could you elaborate on which countries you've allocated that provision?
Because we've seen how Spanish peers aren't really popping up that COVID overlay. It'll be interesting to see if you differ from them. That's it. That's my two questions. Thank you very much.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Thank you, Carlos. Well, M&A appetite, we are not looking. What you mentioned is agreement with OEMs. Well, we look at this as almost as a BAU. If I look backwards in the last year, we signed three important deals. The main one was Stellantis. That was a restructuring of the previous deal that will bring to us. Our portfolio as a result of this will grow in the region of EUR 5 billion with an agreement with Stellantis. We reached another important agreement with Mitsubishi to be the provider in the US. We've done another agreement, very important, this one, with Honda in Mexico to be the provider for Honda in Mexico. Naturally, we have plenty of discussions, in some cases for one country, in some cases for the whole Europe.
Probably we have several of those open, but nothing that I can communicate at this stage because. I see this as a BAU for the division of digital consumer finance. Reaching agreements with the OEMs means, in some cases, that we establish a joint venture with them, in which we match the financial side, and they match the commercial side of the joint venture, or having a white label, providing white label to them and provide our services to their. We agree in this. I forgot to mention that we also reached an agreement in Greece last year with the main importer in Greece that has 30% market share.
This is, as I should say, business as usual, and is in our projections that we gave for the business as usual in the Digital Consumer Bank space. The provisions overlay I said before, but well, this EUR 600 million is, roughly speaking, numbers, EUR 100 million in Spain, EUR 260 million in UK, and EUR 130 million in US. Those are the EUR 600 million that you have embedded due to macro in the H1 results.
Begoña Morenes
Global Head of Investor Relations, Banco Santander
Thank you, José Antonio, and thank you, Carlos, for your question. Can we have the last question, please?
Operator
The last question is coming from Britta Schmidt from Autonomous Research. Please go ahead.
Britta Schmidt
Senior Analyst, Autonomous Research
Yeah. Hi there. Good morning. I've got two questions please. One is on the rate outlook for Brazil. The consensus expects that there will be rate cuts in 2023, and maybe you can help us work through the dynamics of your NII outlook then. Could we see even wider spreads, let's say, in the second half of 2023, depending, of course, on the timing? My second question will be on Poland. Do you have any update on the WIBOR issues there? Do you expect this still to become a legal case and drag on? What's the latest from the ground? Thank you.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
In the rate outlook for Brazil, we expect the rates to peak rather sooner than later, but maybe in August, maybe September this year. While, when those rates start to go down, more difficult to say. As you know, in the very short run, the CFO already elaborate on this. Normally, you should expect one, two quarters negative or positive, and afterwards the commercial dynamics prevail. Yeah. Overall, those are the dynamics and what you should expect from NII. This is the outlook for rates in Brazil while still highly uncertain next year. Yeah. Poland, you're asking me if it's a legal case. It's too early to tell.
While we are, naturally, as of today, analyzing the situation. I provide you the impact, assuming a 50% take-up on the mortgage moratoria. This is a significant damage for the system as a whole. While our colleagues, the financial system in Poland, will take a view on this, while this is not an individual case, this is a whole financial community in Poland that should take the appropriate view on this, when we finish to analyze the proposal from the government.
José García Cantera
CFO and Senior EVP, Banco Santander
Yeah. If I may add, in terms of the WIBOR, we just know that there is a proposal to change it, but we don't have the details. It would start next year, but there are no details at all with regards to the change in the WIBOR. It will be very difficult-
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Very difficult. Yeah.
José García Cantera
CFO and Senior EVP, Banco Santander
To change the index. I don't know if you want to elaborate, but it would go against recommendations for index regulation in Europe, so it would be very difficult to change. We have no news.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
The proposal is difficult to execute. As José said, this European regulations prevent to go this way and that's the situation. We do not expect any news soon, yeah, on this. No. Okay.
Begoña Morenes
Global Head of Investor Relations, Banco Santander
Thank you, José and José Antonio. There are no further questions.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Thank you, guys, and take care.
José García Cantera
CFO and Senior EVP, Banco Santander
Thank you.
José Antonio Álvarez
CEO, Banco Santander
Have good holidays, those who take holidays next couple of weeks. Thank you. Bye.
José García Cantera
CFO and Senior EVP, Banco Santander
Thank you, everybody. Bye.

content.text:
[Company Representative] (Sanofi)
Company Representative, Sanofi
Jean-Baptiste de Chatillon, Chief Financial Officer. For the Q&A, you have two options to participate. Option one, click the Raise Hand icon at the bottom of your screen, or option two, submit your question by clicking the Q&A icon at the bottom of the screen. With that, I'd like to turn the call over to Paul.
Paul Hudson
CEO, Sanofi
Well, thank you, Eva. Great introduction, and thanks to everyone for joining our Call today. Delighted to be here and together with the members of the executive team to take you through the updates on our business and our financial performance. Let's start with Q1 sales view. Well, we're truly excited about the outstanding results in the first quarter. The strong performance of our businesses exceeded market expectations, with 8.6% growth on the top line and EPS up 16.1%. Our Specialty Care business continues to grow at a remarkable pace. Dupixent posted high double-digit growth in the US and strong ex-US sales now annualizing close to EUR 2 billion. We have once again accelerated our critical milestones with several new indications submitted in both the US and EU in pursuit of our greater than EUR 13 billion sales ambition for Dupixent.
Vaccines reported good business momentum with strong growth in PPH and a further recovery in sales of travel and endemic vaccines. In general medicines, our Play to Win strategy continues to pay off. Divesting non-core products and investing in transplants and other selected assets resulted in another quarter of growth for our core assets. Likewise, the consumer health business is executing on the strategy outlined at our Capital Markets Day on 5 February 2023. We delivered double-digit growth rates across all key franchises and more than doubled sales in cough and cold. Moving to slide seven, into the third year now of executing on our Play to Win strategy, the strong set of Q1 results marks another proof point of our focus on growth. The constant improvement of our BOI margin puts us on a clear trajectory to deliver on our mid-term financial targets.
In Q1 2022, EPS grew at double-digit rates once again. R&D spend is now growing again as we rebuild the pipeline following a period of lower R&D investments due to the prioritization within Specialty Care and discontinuation of diabetes and cardiovascular activities. Over the last two years, we increased our spending in R&D by EUR 700 million in a cumulative way, funding the development of our priority assets and our recent bolt-ons and acquisitions such as Principia, Kymab, Kiadis, and Tidal. In the area of immunology, we are striving for industry leadership with an exceptional pipeline. Our pipeline spans across our key priorities, tackling a broad spectrum of diseases with the most promising MOAs and offering modalities from injectable to oral to topical.
In addition to Dupixent as the foundation and the cornerstone in type two inflammatory diseases, we now have 10 molecules in development that could start to enter the market as early as 2025. These programs include potentially transformative medicines in specialty care areas such as dermatology and respiratory, representing highly attractive and growing markets with unmet needs, especially in COPD, where no new mechanisms for disease management have emerged for more than two decades. Our oncology and neurology portfolios continue to expand. We aim to build these into industry-leading pipelines similar to our position in immunology, both through in-house developments and of course by targeted M&A and BD. Advancing to slide nine, I want to highlight some key R&D collaborations added during the quarter, and I'll do that before I hand over to John to give us a quick update.
I would like to briefly mention the collaboration with Blackstone. This deal facilitates the development of Sarclisa's subQ formulation, which serves as another example of prioritization. Partnering Sarclisa going forward allows us to reallocate R&D investments to further expand our pipeline and to strengthen our growth areas. In summary, a really strong Q1 for us here at Sanofi. John, over to you.
John Reed
Global Head of Research and Development, Sanofi
Thank you, Paul. We continue to expand our pipeline through deals that add best-in-class science to our existing capabilities. In Q1, we announced three external collaborations that further supplement our pipeline. First, to build on our momentum with the antibody drug conjugate molecule, tusamitamab ravtansine, our potential first-in-class CEACAM5-targeting ADC that's now in phase III for advanced lung cancer. We announced an exclusive collaboration agreement with Seagen to design and develop ADCs with potent payloads for up to three cancer targets. This collaboration will synergistically combine our proprietary monoclonal antibody technology with Seagen's proprietary ADC technology. Second, with Exscientia, we established a strategic research collaboration to utilize machine learning technologies to accelerate the discovery of precision engineered medicines across oncology and immunology.
We expanded our existing relationship and are now accessing the Exscientia AI-based small molecule drug discovery and their precision medicine platform, spanning from chemical lead identification and optimization through to patient selection. With machine learning, this collaboration promises to accelerate our timelines for drug discovery, while also potentially pointing us to those subsets of patients most likely to benefit. Our third collaboration is with IGM Biosciences. Their technology platform offers an exciting approach to developing multivalent IgM antibodies that can efficiently bind and stimulate the activity of cell surface receptors. This unique platform has the potential to overcome historical limitations of conventional bivalent IgG antibodies when seeking agonists of some class of receptors. We've established an exclusive worldwide collaboration agreement to develop IgM antibody agonists against three oncology targets and three immunology inflammation targets.
For clarity, these are not T-cell engagers, but rather engineered IgM antibodies targeting, in each case, a single cell surface receptor that we wish to activate on certain types of immune cells. Advancing to Slide 10. At Sanofi, we believe in the mission of chasing the miracles of science to improve people's lives. The collaborations depicted on this slide exemplify our journey towards this ambition in the context of childhood cancers. One year ago, Sanofi announced its new corporate social responsibility commitments, which are fully embedded in our Play to Win strategy. Within our strategic CSR pillar of innovating for vulnerable communities, we presented our ambition to develop innovative medicines to eliminate cancer deaths in children. Today, conducting clinical trials for pediatric cancers is challenging due to several factors, including broad heterogeneity in terms of prognosis, molecular features of the tumor pathobiology, current treatment strategies, and scientific objectives.
As a result, the design of clinical trials for pediatric cancers is challenged by several practical issues that must be addressed for ensuring trial feasibility for this vulnerable group of patients. That's why Sanofi has partnered with leading oncology institutions to advance innovative clinical trial designs. Aided by the leadership of our head of oncology development, Peter Adamson, who was previously head of the pediatric oncology group, we move forward with a strong sense of purpose and with the objective of creating real impact for these young patients and their families. Speaking of progress in oncology, on slide 11, I'd like to summarize the advances we are making in building an innovative oncology portfolio, now with 14 molecules in development compared to only five molecules just a few years ago.
Starting with Sarclisa, combined with Revlimid, Velcade, and Dexamethasone in newly diagnosed transplant-ineligible multiple myeloma patients, the event-driven IMROZ trial is expected to read out in H2 this year. Initial data for frontline myeloma patients who are eligible for transplant was shared in a podium presentation at the ASH Congress last year, showing an unprecedented rate of MRD negativity pre-transplant. For amcenestrant, our oral selective estrogen receptor degrader, or SERD, we're pursuing a broad program to assess efficacy and tolerability in different lines of therapy. We started our journey with exploratory phase Ib studies, where we observed excellent tolerability combined with strong efficacy and robust target engagement with a once daily 200mg dose.
As is often the practice in oncology drug development, we took a swing at the late line population of second-line, third-line metastatic breast cancer patients, where most of these women have already failed an aromatase inhibitor combined with a CDK4/6 inhibitor and unfortunately have few treatment options. In the phase II trial we call AMEERA-3, we did not observe a clearly superior efficacy benefit for amcenestrant compared to other endocrine therapies. The full data will be presented at a conference in H2 this year. So I would expect knowing that RSV is a seasonal disease, that we are talking about a launch in 2023 for H1 of Nirsevimab. And I would say from there on, it's only upward.
Paul Hudson
CEO, Sanofi
Thanks, Thomas. I think that's probably a good place to bring us to a conclusion. Thank you to everybody for their questions and for their interest today. Just by way of a few thoughts, strong performance in Q1, you've seen it again. Look forward to updating as we get further into the year. Pipeline progress again, so we're excited about what that's looking like and coming together. Although I don't think we deliberately set out to talk about how well we're now running as an organization, I think it's important to not miss the fact that all of this productivity gains allows us to double down on R&D and to prepare for launches that perhaps didn't exist a few years ago. I think that's getting. That's very exciting for us because it means we can positively surprise.
Thank you to everybody for the time today.

content.text:
Ana Patricia Botín
Executive Chairman, Banco Santander
We have laid these foundations to deliver great value to serve a growing customer base, which is up 30 million customers since 2015, increasing profits and improving profitability. Our ROTE is up close to 170 basis points since 2015, and of course, strengthening our capital base in a very significant way, as well as delivering sustainable returns to our shareholders. Just a couple of numbers on this: We have remunerated shareholders with EUR 19 billion since 2015, and our tangible NAV has grown by EUR 12 billion since then. I'm very pleased to report that a strong 2021 takes us very close to meeting our 2019 investor day targets in spite of the pandemic. Actually, in some cases, we're ahead. We will continue to focus on growth, profitability, and strength, including shareholder remuneration.
We are guiding for 2022 a mid-single-digit revenue growth, a cost-to-income ratio close to 45%, and a return on tangible equity above 13%. We're aiming to keep our fully loaded CET1 at around 12%. We're also aiming to maintain the 40% payout in 2022, of which, as we already said, will be 50% share buybacks and the other 50% in cash. I also want to say that longer term, we aspire to increase our total shareholder remuneration beyond 40% to around 50%, again, through share buybacks and growing our cash dividend whilst maintaining a CET1 of 12%. This would, of course, be subject to future corporate and regulatory decisions and approvals. We'll go to the next slide. You've seen a very strong 2021 result.
Our net profit is actually up 25% from 2019, underlying, in a similar percentage, reflecting, as I said, the strength and resilience of our business model. We onboarded 5 million new customers. We are growing revenues by 7% to over EUR 46 billion. We again increased efficiency and reduced the cost of credit. That's down to just 77 basis points and generating a return to shareholders as measured by tangible NAV per share and cash dividend per share of 11%. Importantly, 2021 was a pivotal year for us in terms of capital. We are at the high end of the range, delivering a 12% CET1 fully loaded. Going forward, as I already said, we expect to keep it at these levels of 12%.
You can hear our P&L here. We have been able to recover, actually more than recover, our pre-pandemic levels of customer activity, in terms of the underlying profit before tax. Again, it's a record high of EUR 15.3 billion. Actually, on the quarter, it's the highest underlying in 12 years, and this is up 21%. Our underlying profit of EUR 8.7 billion, that's up 80% versus last year, 23 compared to 19. This reflects optimal cost of risk, but also very strong execution of what I have said many times is a structural change in our business model. Very importantly, as you can see, revenues are growing more than costs with a positive operating leverage. Very strong capital generation in the year and up to CET1 of 12, even though we had significant regulatory headwinds this year.
Even more important is the strong business momentum, and you can see some examples here. We are moving our business model to more fees, diversifying into different sources of revenue linked to our customer focus. These are only some examples. Loans and deposits are growing, mutual funds are growing at 13%. But in the higher return value-added services, which are really what's adding to our profitability, our POS (point of sale) is up 38%, and insurance premiums are up 12%. Our new Buy Now, Pay Later, this is a business we've built on top of our tech stack, Openbank in Germany. It's going across Europe soon. 2 million customers in the first few months. Debt capital markets, M&A up 16%. This is really important for the future, and these are the businesses in which we're investing more heavily.
José Antonio Álvarez will give you details on the regions later. During the year, we also leveraged the diversification and scale of the group. These are two key elements, and we are working more and more on this key strength of our business model. Operational performance is improving across the board: Europe, North America, and South America. Our Digital Consumer Bank, which, as you know, combines our auto and consumer finance and Openbank, is one of our important growth initiatives. In Europe, we are working really hard to transform the business model. Return on tangible assets is close to 10%. As you can see in the slide, our customer focus is also showing up in better NPS across the different countries. The structural changes have led to cost efficiencies of around EUR 200 million.
This is an area we'll continue to focus on next year. In North America, we generated a return on tangible equity of close to 25%. We are also working on a structural basis in the U.S. I'll give you more details later on. We're really trying very hard to leverage the connectivity across the group, our experience in consumer finance in Europe and Latin America, and other global relationships. Corporate and Investment Banking has also made great progress in North America. In Mexico, we are increasing profitability and being very successful in growing new business, like the auto business organically. South America, again, is a standout performer, with Chile and Brazil being the best banks in terms of profitability in their respective markets, and overall returns of 26%.
We're growing double-digit in terms of revenues, growing in terms of market share, and growing customers in very different segments in all these markets. Our Digital Consumer Bank had another very strong year, producing a return on tangible equity of around 15%. I would like to point to two key numbers in this slide. If you look at the group's customer loans and group underlying profit, you can see Europe is where we have 60% of our loans and 28% of our profits. Again, this means our business is more dependent on lending in Europe. This is something we're working on to increase fees and increase profitability. It also means reduced risk, as a lot of these loans are secured, such as mortgages in countries like the UK and Spain.
In South America, you can see 14% customer loans and 31% underlying profit. This is exactly an example of very positive operating leverage, very diversified businesses, many of them high-growth fee businesses linked to digital initiatives like, you know, auto platforms, Getnet, and other such businesses. The same applies to North America. As you can see, 14% of the loans and 29% of the profits. We have been leading and intend to continue to lead in responsible banking, and here we have very specific targets in terms of our green transition for us and our customers, building a more inclusive society, and of course, talent and diversity. In terms of the green transition, we are working with our customers to help them with that transition. We are focused on delivering on our own net-zero ambition by 2050, which of course includes our customers.
In terms of our own operations, we are already net zero. We are working, again, on the advisory side, on the capital market, but also increasingly developing retail and SME products. We originated EUR 61 billion in green finance in 2019. We have EUR 27 billion under management, and we're the number one bank in project finance in renewable energy. We are, again, making a lot of progress in our very important goal of empowering 10 million individuals by 2025. We're on target to reach that. We've empowered 7 million people in 2019, and also allocated EUR 500 million in microfinance in 2021. As I said before, we are very, very focused and proud to have been the number one bank in the Bloomberg Gender-Equality Index and the number two company worldwide.
This is an area where we'll continue to focus, as we think diversity is not just the right thing; it's also good for business. In summary, responsible banking, we believe, is key to delivering on all our other commitments. We are creating value for our shareholders. We did set a 40% payout of underlying earnings, split in equal parts between cash dividends and also buyback programs. We will be announcing in a couple of weeks the second dividend after the interim dividend of 1.7 EUR, which was half and half between cash and buybacks. We continue to believe buybacks are an excellent investment of our capital, and so that would be the intention for the second dividend as well.
I will now pass over to José Antonio, who's going to review the returns and detailed operating metrics for the year.
José Antonio Álvarez
Spanish banker and former CEO, Banco Santander
Thank you, Ana, and good morning to everyone. As Ana has already commented, we recorded a pretty strong set of results in 2021, with an underlying profit of EUR 8.7 billion, 78% higher year-on-year in constant euros, driven by a very positive performance across the board, notably in the US, UK, Brazil, and the CIB and wealth management businesses. Our net banking income pre-provision profit was around EUR 25 billion, with an increase of 9% year-on-year, which I think is remarkable. This was driven by 7% revenue growth.
Net interest income grew 7% on the back of higher volumes, lower cost of funds, better credit spreads in Latin America, and some positive impact from recent interest rate hikes in some Latin American countries and Poland. Net interest income rose 8% year over year. Double-digit growth occurred in corporates, wholesale banking, and wealth management and insurance due to greater commercial and financial activity. Costs increased at half the pace of the revenue, which has driven significant efficiency improvements. The significant fall in loan loss provision across the group accelerated in Q4, driven by the improvement in the macroeconomic outlook and the very positive performance of our main portfolios.
If we look one step down in the P&L and analyze the quarterly trends in core lines, we saw improving trends across the board on the P&L lines through the year. Q4 was the most profitable quarter of 2021, at EUR 2.3 billion, following a good performance, particularly on the provisioning side. Also, some of the releases were offset by the contribution to the deposit guarantee fund bank levy and the charge for the Swiss francs in Poland. Net-net, the quarter is fairly comparable with the previous ones. In more detail, sustained customer revenue growth, +4% NII, and 3% fee income quarter on quarter, driven by greater volumes, initial impact from interest rate hikes, as I mentioned before, and growth in higher value-added products and services.
Q-on-Q increases in costs are almost fully explained by boundary adjustments, so this does not represent a running rate for the coming year. In addition, a lower loan loss provision in Q4 favored the aforementioned provision release. I will run through the costs and provisions in more detail in the following slides. On the cost side, we have seen significant inflationary pressure around the world. Group costs rose 4% in constant EUR, but were 2% lower in real terms, absorbing higher IT expenses, digital developments, increased activity, and labor agreements that particularly affected the second part of the year. Our efficiency ratio improved to circa 46%. This was basically driven by Europe, minus 5 full percentage points, which has recorded the highest efficiency gains.
I should stress that the cost in Spain went down 7%, in Portugal 5%, and the UK also decreased. There is more to come in 2022, and our running rate will decrease in line with our targets for the region. We continue to make structural changes to our operating model to drive new improvements in productivity, which should enable us to maintain cost growth below inflation and further improve our efficiency rate. On credit quality, the balance sheet remains, I would say, robust. The NPL ratio is 3.16, below 2020 and 2019. Provisions are down 37% in constant EUR, partly due to the releasing of provisions in Q4.
We also significantly reduced the cost of credit, as Ana already mentioned, to 7 basis points below 2020 and 2019 levels, exceeding our initial 2021 target. In 2022, we expect to maintain the cost of credit below our through-the-cycle ratio. Spain will be key as we expect its cost of credit to reduce to approximately 50 basis points, offsetting some normalization in the US and UK. Finally, regarding capital, in 2021, we reached a fully loaded core equity of 11.21%, thanks to the strong operating results we delivered quarter on quarter. In Q4, we generated 42 basis points organically, a combination of net profit, net of dividends, and efficient risk-weighted asset management, as the risk-weighted assets were flat in the quarter.
Negative impacts in the quarter of 2 basis points due to small regulatory impacts. We already spoke about this in the previous quarter. Nine basis points due to market movements affecting some ALCO portfolios, and 5 basis points from the minority interest that's in Mexico. If we include the acquisition of Exclusa that was approved the same week, and was executed the same week, as of 8 basis points, we closed on 31 January 2022, and the announced acquisition of the broker-dealer, Amherst Pierpont, that affects 8 basis points, with this still subject to completion, which will have an impact of 16 basis points on our pro forma CET1 ratio, which will stand at 11.96%. We were able to combine this performance with an increase in the tangible net asset value per share.
Looking at the regions, starting with Europe, we are accelerating our business transformation. This is where we are pushing harder to change our operating model. Profits doubled in the region, reaching EUR 3 billion, with higher profitability due to volume growth, particularly in mortgages, in line with economic recovery. Net operating income was up 24%, supported by wider spreads in most countries. Revenue was up 11%, particularly customer revenue, while costs remained flat due to ongoing efficiency gains. There was a 32% reduction in loan loss provision, and our cost of credit improved to under 40 basis points.
In the following slides, for the sake of clarity, I include the ROTE adjusted to 12% CET1 in all units. We are making this adjustment to allow for a like-for-like comparison between the units, given their very different capital ratios. In Europe, starting with Spain, Spain showed a strong pickup in activity in individuals, mortgages, and consumer lending. Customer funds also grew significantly last year. Profit nearly doubled, boosted by strong net operating income performance. Jaws were 10 percentage points, revenue grew 13%, costs grew 3%, and efficiency gains drove a 7% reduction in cost. Loan loss provisions reduced 8% year on year, and in 2022, we expect to have our cost of credit.
We also expect single-digit balance sheet growth in 2022. In the UK, we improved four-fold. It's a four-fold increase in profit, basically by record net mortgage lending. You don't see this in the loan book that only grows 0.5% due to the fact that we completed the transfer of the CIB business to the London branch, and this affects some of the loan portfolio that went from a ring-fenced bank to the London branch. Plus 22% year-on-year growth in NII due to deposit repricing and volumes on the mortgage that I mentioned before. Cost savings from our transformation program were partially offset by IT investments and regulatory-related programs. Efficiency improved by nearly 11 percentage points. Loan loss provision releases reflecting balance sheet strength. As a result, we achieved double-digit return on tangible equity in the UK.
In North America, we improved our competitive position by increasing connectivity in the region, consolidating IT functions, and advancing significantly in business simplification. We also announced several transactions in 2021, in line with our strategy to deploy capital in the most profitable businesses. Volumes grew, driven by our main segments in both countries. Profit doubled, driven largely by lower provisions and higher revenue in the US. In the US, we had an extremely positive 2021. On a like-for-like basis, excluding Puerto Rico and Bluestem portfolio disposals, loans grew with double-digit growth in auto originations. Customer funds increased due to retail deposits with a significantly lower cost of funding. Underlying profit increased sharply, supported by an 11% increase in net operating income (NII), fees, and auto lease results, and an 85% decline in loan loss provisions.
In short, strong performance, with the US being one of the engines of the group in 2021 results. In Mexico, we increased our stake to over 96% and continue to invest in the franchise, reflecting positive results and customer growth. In a challenging environment, with rate cuts in 2020 and falling volumes, we were able to quickly adapt, resulting in improving trends within the year. As a result, we delivered an 8% increase in profit, thanks to loan and deposit growth, controlled costs well below inflation despite IT investments, and a better cost of credit. Finally, regarding the last region, South America, we continue to strengthen connectivity. We are a market leader across the region. We are capturing synergies across the region and new business opportunities, and boosting our already profitable franchise.
We show strong customer growth in all the countries where we are leaders in quality of service, as measured by NPS. In terms of results in 2021, we delivered greater volumes in all countries, double-digit customer revenue growth, increased productivity with costs growing well below inflation, and a lower cost of credit in all countries. This resulted in strong profit and a very high return on tangible equity. In Brazil, it was another excellent year. Record customer attraction, with more than 5 million customers, translated into significant growth in individuals, loans to individuals growing 22%, consumer finance 12%, and SMEs +15%. This translated into the P&L with a return on tangible equity well above 20%. Double-digit growth in customer revenue and record annual efficiency levels below 30% for the first time. We maintained credit quality at comfortable levels.
In Chile, our digitization process allowed us to significantly increase our customer attraction, which is reflected in the +23% increase in demand deposits and double-digit fee income growth, widening the gap in NPS with our competitors, making us the market leader. We had excellent year-on-year profit performance. NII +10%, improved efficiency, an increasing gap to peers, and a lower cost of credit driven by better-than-expected performance in SMEs and corporates. The consumer bank, the Digital Consumer Bank, had solid balance sheet dynamics. New business activity has recovered to pre-COVID levels, up 10%, despite the challenges posed by COVID restrictions and the semiconductor shortage. Of note was auto, with +13% origination on the back of increasing our market share by 50 basis points across Europe.
Additionally, we are working on the expansion of Openbank, which performed very well in terms of customer increase and volumes this year. Loans grew 48%, and customer funds grew 24%. Total Digital Consumer Bank revenue was boosted by the new business recovery, particularly in consumer leasing. It was a positive year in credit quality, with a further reduction in the cost of credit. In summary, excellent results reflected a 16% underlying profit growth and an increase in profitability return on tangible equity, sitting at 14%. Going to the two businesses we report as secondary segments, both have had a very good year in the industry. For corporate investment banking, revenues grew 10%, a sharp improvement in loan loss provision. We are gaining share, and we are at the top of the market in private finance, top three in private finance in Europe and Latin America.
As Ana mentioned, we are focused on sustainable alternatives and ESG through green financing. We are investing in the business. The cost increased as we are investing in continental Europe, the UK, and the US to develop new capabilities to serve our customers. In wealth management insurance, we saw excellent business performance in 2021. Record commercial flows of EUR 20 billion, with EUR 12 billion in private banking and EUR 8 billion in asset management. Insurance premiums for the protection business increased at double-digit rates. Wealth management insurance's total contribution to the group increased 12% to EUR 2.3 billion. Finally, regarding PagoNXT, we made a commitment to grow the business and revenue by 50%. We achieved EUR 500 million, a 47% increase year-on-year.
In merchant acquiring, Getnet continued to deliver growth, increasing the number of active merchants and total payment volumes by 50%. Getnet Brazil recorded significant market share gains. Getnet Europe started to operate in H2 as a pan-European acquirer following the integration of former Wirecard's technology. In international trade, One Trade currently connects our customers in eight Santander banks, exceeding 8,000 active SMEs and corporates, doubling in size since March. In summary, we have made significant progress in the last 12 months as PagoNXT, as we invest in world-class technology and recruit the best payment talent to continue innovating and launching new products. I hand over the floor to Ana to continue with the presentation.
Ana Patricia Botín
Executive Chairman, Banco Santander
Thank you very much, José Antonio. As I said, we're delivering today, and we're building the Santander of tomorrow. We believe in an era of digital revolution. This is absolutely essential. I have to say, first of all, I am hugely proud of our team and the progress we have made over the last few years. We have laid the foundations to deliver great value and service to our growing customer base, which, as I said, was up 30 million since 2015. We have, at the same time, increased profits, improved our profitability, and strengthened our capital base, as well as delivering sustainable returns to shareholders. I am incredibly excited about what lies ahead. We are continuing our journey to become the best open financial services platform, acting responsibly and earning the lasting loyalty of our people, customers, shareholders, and communities.
This is what is driving our day-to-day across regions and businesses. In our daily work, actually, we're not just, of course, meeting our legal and regulatory expectations. Our aspiration is to exceed all our stakeholders' and our people's expectations. This is a key driver to attract the best talent, which, as we know, is at the basis of success for any company these days. We are focusing on the areas where, as a group, we can have the greatest impact, helping more people and businesses prosper in a way that is simple, personal, and fair. I mentioned earlier our unique business model, delivering more predictable and growing results through the cycle. This is the case not just over the last few years, but over the last 20-25 years.
We have a diversified geographical footprint, which is well-balanced between emerging and developed markets. I would like to note especially the contribution of the US to the group's underlying profit increase from 7% in 2019 to 22% this year. We are building on a global scale, and this is really what's allowing us to grow revenues, but also to expand our business. One great example you have here is Getnet. Getnet is a global platform now operating in six countries. Our global businesses, insurance and corporate banking, continue to add value with very strong revenue growth. Compared to 2019, up 25% for CIB and 12% in wealth management and insurance. These are areas where we're intending to invest more, as they have very high profitability and strong growth.
Importantly, this is a key goal for us across the bank: customer satisfaction. We want customers who love our products. Our NPS is already in the top three in most of our markets, and we intend to continue building on that, improving customer service, and also increasing connectivity. This is one of the, I would say, more difficult but most successful goals we have set for ourselves over the last few years. We are continuing to invest in technology to change our business model, increasing connectivity, not just sharing but building across the group together, creating a better bank. Where do we see the return on these investments? I think these are two key facts you have on the screen over the last two years. This is compared to 2019.
Our digital transactions for our core banks have gone from 55% in 2018-2019 to 76% in 2021. Our digital sales, again across the group, over total sales went from 36% to 54%. I want to stress that in many cases, we are now building global solutions together. I will comment a bit more later, but PagoNXT aims to be a common tech backbone for payments for all our customers across the group, as well as for open markets. At One Santander, we are redefining our own operating model, and I want to give a couple of examples. Our regional consumer finance platform in South America is a single platform for all the countries in South America. In Europe, we have our common app, but also other initiatives to develop key products and drive connectivity where we have horizontal business owners already in place leading for Europe.
In North America, for example, technology is already being shared across the U.S. and Mexico. We've saved $100 million over the last couple of years. Just for 2022, we're aiming for an additional $50 million in this region. Last but not least, our Digital Consumer Bank is re-platforming our legacy auto and consumer services on top of our retail banking native digital Openbank. I want to stress that in this vertical, we're going digital, building our own technology. At the same time, we're maintaining a 14-15% return. I want to now briefly share with you how we're managing our capital allocation and how we're increasing the discipline every year. We today have the tools to manage our capital in a very granular way.
You can see here that in 2021, we had 30% of our RWA below the cost of equity. We're aiming to have 20% in 2022. Of course, these are businesses where we're investing for the future. I want to say that in 2015, that thirty was 60%. We've been ruthless in this discipline. We intend to continue to manage in this way going forward. We will allocate more capital, as we have done over the last few years, to our most profitable and higher-growing geographies, segments, and businesses. We're expecting RWAs to expand at lower rates than loans again in 2022.
We again have a target for our front book not to have assets going on the books, on average across the bank, below 2.2 in 2022 compared to 1.8, and we'll continue to actively manage our underperforming portfolios, as I mentioned. We are also making some accretive investments. Of course, there are the offers to buy minorities we've done. We did Brazil at the end of 2014. We've done Mexico and Santander Consumer, as José Antonio mentioned, which actually closed this Monday, two days ago. We also still have the acquisition of Amherst Pierpont pending closing. That's pending regulatory approval, but this is incredibly accretive to us, and the connectivity with our CIB franchises across Europe and the Americas is really important.
In every case, in these acquisitions, we are always seeing returns on investment above our cost of capital. Again, we continue to expect strong and actually growing organic capital generation. This is based on solid growth, optimal return on risk, and ROTEs above 13%, keeping fully loaded at 12%, so we can continue to grow in the future, increasing shareholder returns going forward. As a summary, a strong focus on capital discipline will be key. We have done it in 2021. We aim to deliver tangible net asset value per share growth, growing cash dividends, and profitability. Growing cash dividends as profitability improves, and making sure buybacks are a meaningful part of our remuneration strategy.
We continue to target a 40% payout ratio, even though in the future we would aim to increase that to 50%, again, subject to board approval and the performance of the bank. Longer term, this is the intention, and very importantly, we aim to keep our CET1 at the 12% level, as I mentioned. How are we going to deliver on these goals? We want to continue to deliver on our business model. We are working on increased connectivity, our three strategic initiatives, which I will mention briefly now: One Santander, PagoNXT, and the Digital Consumer Bank, all of which are providing a distinctive competitive advantage because we're building a globally recognizable brand that customers trust and value, at the same time, improving profitability.
First with One Santander, this is the way we are building, first regionally, but also from today across the global footprint. Shared services, I mentioned Latin America and consumer finance, but there are many others, our European operating hubs. We're aiming first and foremost to improve customer experience, but to do that in an efficient, profitable way. These are the targets for Europe: again, structural change while delivering sustainable profitability. This covers the four countries: Spain, UK, Portugal, and Poland. We are very confident that this turnaround, which you've seen already some of those numbers this year. For individuals, the focus will be enhancing digital, but always building on that personal and digital combination. We are working through PagoNXT on delivering differentiated cross-border services for SMEs.
We also announced EUR 1 billion in cost synergies by the end of 2022. We remain committed to that. Obviously, it's going to be a bit more challenging given the inflationary environment. We're expecting some tailwinds for 2022, so normalizing the cost of risk by 2023. In addition, we'll continue to reallocate capital not just among segments and countries, but also into more profitable and higher-growth businesses. In North America, we expect to develop and work further on the synergies on the back of that cross-border US-Mexico, but also across the group's opportunities. Operational efficiencies will be meaningful. We are now working. Actually, we already have the plans in place. We got approval yesterday to manage the business in a different way. I will comment on that in a few minutes. We launched the US-Mexico business corridor a few years ago.
We're generating very high growth in cross-border customers. Just as an example, total revenue had a 20% increase year-on-year in this business, and we're aiming to continue that growth. The aim for the region would be around 20% ROTE and an efficiency of 44. In the US, and I want to focus on the consumer side, the goal is to simplify the bank and really build a consumer auto business, leveraging what we have done in Europe and also in Latin America, but also on the very strong Santander consumer franchise and the core deposits in our retail bank. Amherst Pierpont, again, is going to allow us to deliver for many more customers.
The connectivity is already great, around 10%, for example, in our wealth management customers in the US have been referred by our bankers in other geographies, and this is a business where we can actually grow much faster. In Mexico, again, accelerating growth, improving profitability, where we have been investing in technology together with the US for the last couple of years. Just a bit more detail on the US and how we are looking at the business. I want to just remind everyone that for a few years, we were very much focused on, and of course, that will continue to be a focus, but now we can focus on growth and on the management of the business, which is aligned to the US peers. The consumer business will be focused on a consumer model, much like the Digital Consumer Bank is in Europe.
We'll be leveraging two very key group assets. One is technology, and the second is our OEM experience and relationships across the world. This year, we delivered a 24% return on equity, actually a bit above that. For next year, the goal is 19% with efficiency around 43. Simplification is going to be key. We're actually exiting some businesses in the US, like home equity and mortgages, to really simplify the bank based on what we believe we need to support our retail customers and the consumer business. In terms of CRE and multifamily, we're top 10 in the US, very profitable through the cycle, funded by commercial deposits. CIB, I mentioned already.
We see a lot of upside in, you know, low-risk customer-based businesses where Amherst Pierpont adds a significant investor, institutional customer base. The leading brands we have in all of Latin America in high net worth. Again, there's many opportunities here for add-on businesses where we are investing, and we believe this is gonna be one of our drivers of growth. By the way, we're working sometime in Q2 to have a more detailed meeting with investors on our strategy in the US, giving you more detail on how it is that we're gonna execute in this key market for us. South America, again, strong growth in customers and revenues. We remain absolutely confident that the region is a high-growth opportunity, delivering through the cycle.
One key aspect is the growth of the middle class in many of these markets. That is the key to the expanding demand for our services. We are expecting double-digit growth in retail. We will consolidate more and more operations across the region, in many of the verticals. We believe there's a lot of value operating as a single bank with a regional approach, and building all the connectivity that I described. In corporates, just to give you an example, we're growing by around 25% with the Multilatinas. That's a EUR 250 million business today, of course, with very strong opportunities also with Amherst Pierpont in terms of accessing dollar markets.
In wealth, the connection with our bank in Miami is a key differentiator for us, and in global businesses, and here I mean cards and payments, again, building on the global platforms. All of that leading to a regional return on tangible equity of around 25%, and that is in spite of the cyclical currency depreciation, with a current efficiency of around 35%. Let me briefly turn to PagoNXT. This is a very strategic initiative. Payments are at the heart of our customers' banking relationships. It's key for our loyalty strategy. That's not new. It has happened for many years. Now it's turning digital, and scale becomes crucial. Again, this is a high-growth, high-profitability business. I want to say that as we build this platform, we're also delivering revenue growth.
We're very pleased with the progress that PagoNXT has made this year. We're investing to integrate all these payment systems to benefit the scale across the Santander banks, but especially customers and the open market, as you can see in the slide.
